stages.title: Oceanography fundamentals
stages.hook: The ocean looks blue and flat from a beach. What is hiding below the surface, and how would you measure it?
explain: Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface. The average depth is roughly 3.7 km, and the deepest place, Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, is nearly 11 km down. Oceanography is the science that studies all this.

Sea water is salty because rivers and rocks add dissolved salts, and when water evaporates the salt stays behind. Typical sea water has about 35 grams of salt in every kilogram of water. Salty water is denser than fresh water.

Conditions change with depth. Sunlight reaches only the top 200 m or so, the sunlit zone. Below that it is dark and cold. Pressure grows by about 1 bar for every 10 m of depth, so engineers must build deep-sea equipment very strong.

example.q: A scientist takes 4 kg of sea water with 35 g of salt per kg. How much salt is in the sample?

analogies.home: Stirring salt into a glass of water is like what happens naturally in the sea, only on a gigantic scale.
analogies.sport: Diving deep is like going down a very long slide where the push on your body gets bigger each metre.
analogies.nature: Plants grow only where light reaches, so most sea plants live near the surface.
analogies.tech: Sonar works like a bat's call: send a sound, listen for the echo, and work out the depth.

stages.mnemonic: Sun, Twilight, Midnight: light gets less and pressure gets more as you go down.
terms: How much dissolved salt is in the water.
A very deep, narrow valley in the sea floor.
The top layer of the ocean where light can reach.
Using sound echoes to measure depth or find objects.

misc.wrong: Deep water is just like shallow water, only deeper.
misc.right: Deep water is darker, colder and under far greater pressure, which changes both life and engineering.

stages.limits: Salinity is not the same everywhere: it is lower near big river mouths and melting ice, and higher in hot dry seas. Depth figures are measured values that are refined over time.

trip.prompt: Find the ocean zones diagram and note how deep each layer starts.

questions.why: Plants need light to make food, and light fades out below about 200 m.

questions.q: A ship sends a sound pulse down and hears the echo 2 seconds later. Explain how this tells the sailors the depth.
questions.model: Sound travels down, bounces off the sea floor and comes back. Knowing the speed of sound in water and the time, you work out the distance. You halve it because the sound went down and back.
questions.why: Depth = speed × time ÷ 2, because the echo travels to the bottom and returns.

panel.q: Near the mouth of a large river the sea is less salty than far out. Why?
o: Fresh river water mixes in and dilutes the salt
Fish remove salt from the water as they swim and breathe
The sun removes salt from the water near the shore

panel.why: Fresh water lowers the amount of salt per kilogram.

o: It is less dense
It is heavier
It is darker
It is faster
panel.why: Fresh and warmer water is less dense, so it sits above denser salty water.

panel.q: Why is it important for engineers to know the depth and conditions of the sea before building something?
panel.model: Depth, pressure, waves and currents decide how strong a structure must be. Measuring them first helps engineers design something safe that will not fail or harm the sea.
panel.why: Design loads come from the environment, so surveys keep people and the ocean safe.

teach.topic: What is special about the deep ocean
teach.model: The ocean is salty, dark and cold below the top layer, and the deeper you go the greater the pressure. Light reaches only about 200 m. Machines must be strong to go down there.

Can sunlight get all the way down?
What does that mean for machines?

stages.title: Buoyancy and hydrostatics
stages.hook: Why does a steel ship float but a steel nail sinks? Predict, then find out what really decides it.
explain: Hydrostatics is the study of water that is not moving. In still water, pressure depends on depth: p = ρ × g × h, where ρ (rho) is the density of the water, g = 9.81 m/s² and h is the depth. In this course sea water has density 1025 kg/m³.

Archimedes' principle says that the upward buoyant force on an object equals the weight of the water it pushes aside: F = ρ × g × V, where V is the volume under water. A floating ship pushes aside exactly its own weight of water.

So a nail sinks because its small volume displaces less water weight than its own weight. A ship has a huge hollow hull, so it displaces a huge volume of water and the buoyant force equals its weight. Weight acts down and buoyancy acts up. If they are equal, it floats.

example.q: A boat displaces 2 m³ of sea water (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²). What is the buoyant force?

analogies.home: Push a beach ball into a bath. The deeper you push, the more water it moves and the harder it pushes back.
analogies.sea: A loaded cargo ship sits lower than an empty one. It needs to push aside more water to hold the extra weight.
analogies.sport: A swimmer who takes a deep breath floats better because the lungs add volume without adding much weight.
analogies.nature: A seal's blubber is light and helps it stay near the surface when it rests.

stages.mnemonic: Float means weight down = push up. The push is the weight of the water moved.
terms: Mass per unit volume, in kg/m³.
The water pushed aside by a floating object.
The upward force from the fluid on an object.
Pressure in still water, p = ρgh.

misc.right: An object floats if its average density is less than the water's, or if it pushes aside its own weight of water. A heavy steel ship does this by being hollow.

stages.limits: We treat the sea as still with constant density. In real seas, waves, temperature and salinity change things a little. We also use gauge pressure, ignoring the air above.

trip.prompt: Find the simple diagram of a floating object. Spot the two forces that balance.

Both the same

It rises higher because it is heavier
Nothing changes because buoyancy stays the same

questions.why: Extra weight needs extra buoyancy, so it must displace more water.

questions.why: A floating boat displaces its own mass of water: 800 ÷ 1025 = 0.7805 m³.

questions.q: Match each quantity to its unit.
questions.why: These are SI units.

questions.q: Explain why a steel nail sinks but a steel ship floats.
questions.model: The ship's hollow shape lets it push aside a huge volume of water, whose weight equals the ship's weight, so buoyancy balances weight. The nail is solid and small, so it displaces far less water than its own weight.
questions.why: Floating depends on average density and displaced volume, not on the material alone.

panel.q: A diver doubles her depth. How does the water pressure from depth change?
o: The gauge pressure doubles
It stays the same
It halves
It becomes four times bigger
panel.why: p = ρgh is proportional to depth.

panel.q: A boat with a small hole fills with water and sinks. Which explanation is best?
o: Water replaces air, raising weight and lowering displacement above the surface
Buoyancy turns off whenever there is a hole in the hull
The sea pulls harder on a boat once it is damaged
The boat becomes steel and so heavier than water
panel.why: The boat's average density rises above that of water as air is lost.

panel.q: Why does a ship carrying heavy cargo have a load line mark painted on the hull?
panel.model: The load line shows the deepest the ship may sit in different waters. Loading beyond it leaves too little height above the water and the ship may be swamped or become unsafe.
panel.why: Load lines protect ships from overloading and set safe limits for fresh and salt water.

teach.model: Water pushes up on a ship with a force equal to the weight of the water the ship moves aside. A ship is hollow so it moves aside a lot of water, and the push matches its weight, so it floats.

points.ask: So why can a heavy ship float?
Why does a nail sink then?

stages.title: Ship geometry
stages.hook: How would you describe the size and shape of a ship using only a few numbers?
explain: Naval architects describe a hull with a few main dimensions. Length (L) is how long, beam (B) is the greatest width, depth (D) is the height from keel to deck, and draught (T) is how far the hull sits below the waterline. Freeboard is the part of the side above the water: freeboard = depth − draught.

Hulls are not boxes. The block coefficient C_B = V ÷ (L × B × T) compares the real underwater volume V with the box that would just hold it. A fat tanker may have C_B near 0.8; a slim fast ferry maybe 0.5.

Displacement is the weight of water the hull pushes aside, which equals the ship's weight when floating. Mass displaced = V × ρ. Ship plans use curves and sections, called the lines plan, to draw the curved shape.

example.q: A barge is 40 m long, 10 m wide and has a draught of 2 m. Its C_B is 0.9. What is its underwater volume?

analogies.home: A shoebox is a box with C_B = 1. A rounded bowl of the same size holds less, like a ship with a smaller C_B.
analogies.city: A road map's contour lines are like a lines plan: lines that show a curved shape on a flat page.
analogies.farm: A tractor's width decides which gate it can pass, as beam decides which lock or dock a ship can use.
analogies.sea: A deeply loaded ship has a bigger draught, like a sailor who carries a heavy bag and stands deeper in mud.

stages.mnemonic: L B D T: Long, Broad, Deep, Tucked-into-water. Freeboard is the dry height left.
terms: How deep the hull sits below the waterline.
The greatest width of the ship.
Height of the side above the water.
Underwater volume divided by L × B × T.

misc.wrong: Draught is the same as the ship's total height.
misc.right: Draught is only the part below the water. Depth is the height of the hull from keel to deck.

stages.limits: Different standards measure length in different ways, such as overall length or length between perpendiculars. Always say which one you use.

stages.title: Ship stability
stages.hook: Why does a ship rock back upright after a wave, while a badly loaded one can roll over?
explain: Every ship has a centre of gravity G, where its weight seems to act, and a centre of buoyancy B, the centre of the displaced water, where buoyancy seems to act. When the ship heels (tilts), B moves sideways because the underwater shape changes.

The metacentre M is the point where the vertical line through the new B crosses the ship's centreline for small tilts. The distance GM is the metacentric height. If M is above G, GM is positive and the ship tends to come back upright: it is stable. GM = KM − KG, where K is the keel.

The righting lever GZ ≈ GM × sin θ for small angles θ. A bigger GM gives a bigger righting force but a quicker, snappier roll. Putting heavy cargo high raises G and cuts GM. Loose liquid in a tank slops to one side (free surface effect), making the ship less stable. Crews must load and secure cargo carefully.

example.q: KM = 8.0 m and KG = 6.5 m. Find GM. Is the ship stable?
steps: GM is positive, so M is above G.

analogies.home: A tall stack of books topples easily; a low, wide stack stays up, like a ship with a low G.
analogies.sport: A cyclist keeps weight low and over the wheels to stay balanced.
analogies.sea: A tall-sided ferry full of cars on the top deck may tip more easily than one with cars on the bottom.
analogies.farm: A tractor with a full load of hay piled high can tip on a slope, like a top-heavy ship.

stages.mnemonic: G low, GM go: keep the weight low and the ship will not roll.
terms: The point where the whole weight seems to act.
The centre of the displaced water.
Distance between G and M; a measure of initial stability.
Loose liquid sloshing, which reduces stability.

misc.wrong: A bigger GM is always better.
misc.right: Too large a GM makes a ship roll quickly and stiffly, which is uncomfortable and can strain cargo. Designers want enough GM but not too much.

stages.limits: GM only works for small tilts. At large angles we use the full GZ curve. Real ships must also pass rules for damage and wind.

questions.q: A ferry has cars parked on its top deck, and passengers all rush to one side. Explain why this is dangerous.
questions.model: Heavy cars high up raise the centre of gravity and reduce GM. Passengers rushing to one side move weight sideways and make the ship heel. A ship with low stability might tip too far and capsize.

panel.q: If a ship's GM is slightly negative, what is a safe action?
o: Lower weight, e.g. fill low ballast tanks, and avoid sharp turns
Add cargo on the top deck
Sail faster
Empty the double bottom
panel.why: Lowering G restores positive GM, and avoiding heeling forces keeps it safe.

teach.model: A ship has a centre of gravity G where its weight acts and a centre of buoyancy B where the push of the water acts. When it tilts, B moves toward the low side and pushes the ship back up, if G is low enough. Putting weight high makes it less stable.

stages.title: Wave properties
stages.hook: Two waves cross the sea. One is long and slow, the other short and choppy. What numbers would you use to tell them apart?
explain: A wave has height H (crest to trough), wavelength λ (distance between two crests) and period T (time for two crests to pass a point). Frequency f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitude is half the height.
The speed of the wave shape is c = λ ÷ T. For deep-water waves, gravity sets the relation: λ = g T² ÷ (2π), about 1.56 T² metres when T is in seconds. So longer-period waves are longer and faster.

Water particles in deep water move in circles, not along with the wave. The motion fades with depth and is small below about half a wavelength. Wind makes waves larger when it blows harder, for longer, and over a longer distance (the fetch). Swell is waves that have travelled far from where they began.

example.q: Waves have wavelength 60 m and period 6 s. What is their speed?

analogies.sport: In a stadium wave, the shape moves round the ground but each fan only stands and sits.
analogies.music: Frequency is like pitch. A short-period wave is a high note, a long one a low note.
analogies.home: Flick one end of a skipping rope and a bump runs along it while the rope itself stays in place.
analogies.sea: A cork rides up and down on a swell and ends close to where it started.

stages.mnemonic: Wave speed: wavelength over time, c = λ/T. Height is crest to trough.
terms: Time for one full wave to pass a point.
The distance wind blows over water.
Smooth waves that have travelled out of the storm that made them.

misc.wrong: The water travels along with the wave.
misc.right: The wave shape travels, but each bit of water mostly moves in a small circle.

stages.limits: The deep-water formula only works when the water is deeper than about half a wavelength. In shallow water waves slow down and the formula changes. Real seas are mixtures of many waves.

panel.q: A wave in deep water has twice the height. What is the effect on its speed?

panel.q: A ship's captain sees waves with a long period. What does this suggest about the wave's source?

A local breeze made it a few minutes ago

panel.why: Long-period swell comes from far-off storms.

panel.q: Why are waves dangerous for small boats near a rocky shore?
panel.model: Waves slow and rise in shallow water near shore, becoming steeper and breaking. A small boat can be flipped or pushed onto rocks.
panel.why: Shoaling makes waves taller and steeper, and breaking waves carry strong force.

teach.model: A wave has a height, a wavelength between crests and a period, the time between crests. Speed is wavelength divided by period. Wind makes waves, and they can travel far as swell.

stages.title: Ocean currents and tides
stages.hook: Twice a day the sea rises and falls on the same beach. Who is pulling the sea?
explain: Tides are the rise and fall of sea level caused mainly by the Moon's gravity, with a smaller pull from the Sun. Most places have about two high tides and two low tides each lunar day of about 24 h 50 min, so high tides are roughly 12 h 25 min apart. The tidal range is the height difference between high and low water.

When the Sun, Earth and Moon line up (new and full Moon) the pulls add together and we get large spring tides. At the half Moons the pulls partly cancel and we get small neap tides. The word spring has nothing to do with the season.

Currents are streams of water in the sea. Surface currents are driven by wind and by Earth's rotation, like the Gulf Stream. Tidal currents flow in and out as the tide rises and falls. Deep currents are driven by differences in density. Engineers must know both when they plan routes, moorings and structures.

example.q: High water is 4.2 m and the next low water is 0.8 m. What is the tidal range?

analogies.home: Tilting a tray of water makes water slosh to one end, something like the Moon making a bulge of water.
analogies.sport: In a tug of war the strongest pull wins, like the Moon's pull stronger than the Sun's on our tides.
analogies.city: The tide coming in and out of a harbour is like a daily commuter flow.
analogies.nature: A river carries a leaf along; an ocean current carries floating seeds across the sea.

stages.mnemonic: Moon makes the Tide; New and Full are Spring-y big, half Moons give the Neap.
terms: Difference in height between high and low water.
A large tide at new or full Moon.
A small tide at the half Moon.

misc.wrong: Tides are caused by the Sun heating the sea.
misc.right: Tides are caused mostly by the Moon's gravity (and the Sun's gravity to a lesser degree), not by heat.

stages.limits: Tide size and timing depend a lot on local coast shape. Some places, such as parts of the Gulf of Mexico, have only one tide a day. Predictions are tables made from local records.

trip.prompt: Find the diagram of spring and neap tides and see where the Sun and Moon sit.

questions.q: What mainly causes tides?
o: Gravity of the Moon and Sun
Wind blowing across the sea all day long
Fish moving together in big groups
Ships pushing water as they pass by
questions.why: The Moon's gravity (mostly) pulls the ocean.

questions.q: When do spring tides happen?
o: At new and full Moon
In spring only, when the weather is warmer
At the half Moon, when the Moon is straight up
Only at night, when the Sun is behind the Earth
questions.why: When Sun and Moon pull in line, tides are largest.

questions.q: A harbour has water 6 m deep at high tide and 2 m at low tide. A ship needs 4 m. When can it safely leave?
o: Around high water
Only at low water
Any time
Never
questions.why: Only near high tide is there enough depth for the draught, plus a safety margin.

questions.q: Which current is driven by differences in density?
o: Deep ocean currents
Wind-driven surface currents
Waves
A river
questions.why: Cold salty water sinks and drives deep flows.

questions.q: A ship moves against a strong tidal current. What happens to its speed over the ground?
o: It is reduced
It increases
It is unchanged
It becomes zero always
questions.why: The water moves backward relative to the ground, so ground speed is lower.

questions.q: High water is 5.6 m and low water is 1.1 m. What is the tidal range in metres?
A current flows at 0.5 m/s. How far does a drifting buoy move in 1 hour (3600 s), in metres?
questions.why: Distance = speed × time = 0.5 × 3600 = 1800 m.

questions.q: Order the tide stages in one cycle, starting at low water.
questions.why: The tide rises (flood) to high water, then falls (ebb).

questions.q: Match each word to its meaning.
questions.why: Standard tide terms.

questions.q: Why should a beach walker check the tide table before walking around a headland?
questions.model: A rising tide can cover the beach and cut off the way back. Checking the table lets you know when high water arrives so you leave in plenty of time.
questions.why: Tides can trap people; planning around them is safe action.

panel.q: Why are tides on average about 50 minutes later each day?
o: The Moon moves around the Earth, so a lunar day is about 24 h 50 min
The sea is lazy and slows down each day
Tides follow the Sun exactly and so never change
Clocks run slowly near the sea so tides seem later
panel.why: The Moon orbits in the same direction as Earth spins, so each place faces it about 50 min later each day.

panel.q: A narrow bay has a very large tidal range. Why do engineers care?
o: Strong currents and large water-level change affect moorings and structures
Waves vanish completely in narrow bays
Fish disappear and the bay loses all its life
Pressure is zero at the bottom of such a bay
panel.why: Large ranges produce strong tidal flow and big changes in water depth.

panel.q: Do ocean currents like the Gulf Stream affect climate?
o: Yes, they carry heat from one place to another
No, they only move fish from place to place
Only in winter, when the wind is strong
Only deep underwater, so the air is never affected
panel.why: Currents move warm or cold water and change nearby coastal climate.

teach.model: The Moon's gravity pulls on the ocean, and the Sun pulls a bit too, so the sea rises and falls about twice a day. When the Sun and Moon line up the tides are bigger. Currents are separate flows of water driven by wind or density.

points.ask: Is a current the same as a tide?

stages.title: Marine structures
stages.hook: How can a wall or a pier stand for years in a place where waves hit it again and again?
explain: Marine structures stand in or beside the sea. Examples are breakwaters, seawalls, jetties, piers, quays, lighthouses and bridges. They protect coasts, shelter harbours or let ships load.

The sea attacks structures in several ways. Waves push and make the structure shake, currents push, wind pushes, and salt water causes corrosion in steel and damage in concrete. Repeated small loads cause fatigue, tiny cracks that grow with each wave.

Engineers design for these loads. Rubble-mound breakwaters use heaps of rock or concrete blocks that break up waves. Piled jetties stand on steel or concrete piles driven into the sea bed. Deck level must be above the highest tide plus the wave crest plus a safety margin.

example.q: Highest tide is 3.0 m above datum, wave crest adds 2.0 m, and a 1.0 m safety margin is needed. Where should the deck be?

analogies.home: Wearing away rocks at the shoreline is like water slowly eroding a sandcastle.
analogies.farm: A breakwater is like a thick hedge that slows the wind and protects crops behind it.
analogies.city: A quay is like a platform at a station where ships stop.
analogies.sport: A goalkeeper's wall must be solid to stop many shots, as a seawall must stop many waves.

stages.mnemonic: Wave, current, wind, salt: four attackers, and engineers add a margin.
terms: A barrier that reduces wave energy in a harbour.
A structure that sticks out into the water for boats.
A long post driven into the sea bed to support a structure.
Slow damage to metal from chemical reaction, e.g. rust.

misc.wrong: A bigger, harder wall always stops waves best.
misc.right: Smooth hard walls can reflect waves and make strong scouring in front. Rough, sloping rock structures absorb wave energy better.

stages.limits: Design waves come from statistics, such as a once-in-100-years storm. Climate change can change those numbers, so designs may be updated.

trip.prompt: Look at a rubble-mound breakwater photo. How might gaps between the rocks help?

questions.q: What does a breakwater do?
o: Reduces waves reaching a harbour
Makes electricity from the waves for the town
Catches fish as they swim into the harbour
Raises the tide inside the harbour
questions.why: It breaks up and absorbs wave energy.

questions.q: What is a pile?
o: A long post driven into the sea bed
A heap of sand piled on the beach
A sail that catches the wind on a boat
A type of wave that breaks near a pier
questions.why: Piles carry the load of a pier or jetty into the ground.

questions.q: Why are steel parts in the sea painted or protected?
o: To slow corrosion from salt water
To make them heavier
To help them float
To warm the water
questions.why: Salt water speeds up corrosion; coatings and anodes slow it.

questions.q: A pier is hit by tens of thousands of small waves every year. Which failure is most linked to this?
o: Fatigue cracking
Melting when the sun heats the steel
Evaporation of the steel into the air
Freezing of the metal in the cold water
questions.why: Repeated loading makes tiny cracks grow, even if each load is small.

questions.q: Why do some seawalls have curved or stepped faces?
o: To redirect or absorb wave energy
To look pretty for people walking along them
To make fish happy and bring more of them
To increase corrosion so the stone wears evenly
questions.why: Shape controls how waves break or are turned back.

questions.q: Highest tide is 2.5 m above datum, a wave crest adds 1.5 m, and the safety margin is 0.8 m. What deck level in metres is needed?
A rock breakwater is 100 m long with a cross-section of 20 m². How many cubic metres of rock does it hold?
questions.why: Volume = area × length = 20 × 100 = 2000 m³.

questions.q: Match each structure to its main job.
questions.why: Each has a different purpose.

questions.q: Put these in a sensible order for building a jetty.
questions.why: Know the site, design, then build from the bottom up.

questions.q: Why does a harbour wall need regular inspections even if it looks fine?
questions.model: Waves, salt and currents slowly cause cracks, corrosion and erosion that may be hidden. Regular checks find problems early so they can be repaired before a storm makes the wall fail.
questions.why: Hidden slow damage can lead to sudden failure in a storm, so early detection is safe action.

panel.q: A new breakwater is built and a beach nearby loses sand. What is a good explanation?
o: It changed the way waves and currents move sand
Sand evaporates into the air in the sun
The beach is angry at the new building
Fish eat the sand from the sea bed at night
panel.why: Structures change coastal sediment movement, sometimes causing erosion.

panel.q: Why are marine plans checked for harm to sea life?
o: Building can disturb habitats and water quality
To waste time before the work can start
Habitats help engineers by building the wall for them
Sea animals do not matter to a building plan
panel.why: Environmental assessment helps reduce harm to ocean life.

panel.q: A designer adds a safety margin to the deck height. Why?
o: Real waves and tides may be higher than predicted
To spend more money than the project needs
To avoid using steel in the deck
Margins make the waves smaller when they arrive
panel.why: Natural conditions vary, so margins allow for uncertainty.

teach.model: Structures like breakwaters and jetties are hit by waves, currents, wind and salt water. Engineers design them strong enough, protect steel from corrosion, and check them often because repeated waves cause tiny cracks.

points.ask: What does salt water do to steel?
What do many small waves do over time?
How do engineers keep them safe?

stages.title: Offshore equipment
stages.hook: An offshore platform has a drilling tower, a flare, a crane and a huge steel frame. Why does each one need to be there?
explain: The main steel frame that stands in the sea is the jacket. It supports the topsides, the decks on top that hold the equipment, living quarters and helideck. A derrick holds the drill string, which is lengths of pipe that drill into the sea bed.

Safety equipment is vital. The blowout preventer (BOP) is a stack of strong valves that can close a well fast if pressure rises dangerously. A flare burns off gas that cannot be used safely. Cranes lift supplies from supply boats, and each has a safe working load (SWL) that must never be exceeded.

Steel in the sea is protected from corrosion by paint and by sacrificial anodes, blocks of metal like zinc or aluminium that corrode instead of the steel. Lifeboats, alarms and strict permits keep the crew safe.

example.q: A crane lifts a 2000 kg container. What is its weight in newtons (g = 9.81 m/s²)?

analogies.home: A sacrificial anode is like a decoy: the plate that rusts first protects the pipe, like a fuse that blows first.
analogies.city: Topsides are like a small factory on top of a bridge.
analogies.farm: A crane is like a tractor loader, always with a limit to what it can lift.
analogies.tech: A blowout preventer is like a huge emergency stop button for a well.

stages.mnemonic: Jacket holds, topsides work, BOP stops, anode sacrifices.
terms: A steel frame fixed to the sea bed that supports a platform.
The decks and equipment above the waves.
Strong valves that seal a well in an emergency.
A metal block that corrodes instead of the steel it protects.

misc.wrong: A crane can lift anything if the hook is strong enough.
misc.right: A crane has a safe working load that depends on its reach, angle and the sea state. Overloading can tip or break it.

stages.limits: Not all platforms use jackets. Floating platforms use hulls and moorings instead. Exact equipment depends on whether the field produces oil, gas or wind power.

trip.prompt: Find a labelled picture of a platform. Spot the derrick, flare, crane and jacket.

questions.q: What is the jacket of an offshore platform?
o: A steel frame fixed to the sea bed
A life vest that workers wear in a storm
A sail fitted to the top of the platform
A cargo ship that carries supplies to it
questions.why: The jacket supports the topsides above the waves.

questions.q: What is the job of a blowout preventer?
o: Seal the well in an emergency
Pump fish
Light the deck
Hold the crane
questions.why: It closes valves to stop uncontrolled flow.

questions.q: Why are anodes made of zinc or aluminium attached to steel in the sea?
o: They corrode first and protect the steel
They make steel float on the surface
They make a noise that scares fish away
They cool the water around the steel parts
questions.why: They are more reactive than steel so they corrode instead.

questions.q: A crane has a safe working load of 10 t. A crew wants to lift 12 t. What is the right action?
o: Do not lift; split the load or use a bigger crane
Lift it quickly
Lift it in rough weather
Ignore the limit
questions.why: Exceeding SWL risks collapse.

questions.q: Why is waste gas burned in a flare instead of just released?
o: Burning is safer than letting flammable gas build up
It makes the sea warmer for the fish nearby
It helps fish by lighting up the water at night
Gas is useless and has to be got rid of anyway
questions.why: Gas can explode if it collects; flaring removes it safely, though it still releases carbon dioxide.

questions.q: A crane lifts a 2000 kg container. Use g = 9.81 m/s². What is the weight in newtons?
A drill string is made of 30 lengths of pipe, each 9.5 m long. How long is the string in metres?
Match each item to its job.
questions.why: Each part has a clear task.

questions.q: Order the parts from the sea bed upwards.
questions.why: Piles hold the jacket, which holds the topsides.

questions.q: Explain why offshore crews must follow strict rules (permits) before hot work like welding.
questions.model: Sparks can ignite flammable gas and cause fire or explosion. On a remote platform escape is hard, so permits and gas checks make sure the work is safe before starting.
questions.why: Remote locations and flammable material make careful procedures essential.

panel.q: A sacrificial anode is almost used up. What should the inspection team do?
o: Replace it before the steel loses protection
Ignore it
Paint it
Add a heavier crane
panel.why: When the anode is gone, the steel begins to corrode.

panel.q: Why is the crane's safe working load lower in rough seas when lifting from a supply boat?
o: Boat motion adds dynamic loads
Water is heavier in rough seas than in calm seas
Gravity changes when the sea is rough
Cranes get tired when the boat moves a lot
panel.why: A moving boat can jerk the load and add extra force.

panel.q: Which is the best response to an oil spill on the deck near drains?
o: Contain and clean it so it does not reach the sea
Hose it into the sea
Cover with a mat only
Ignore it
panel.why: Containment protects the ocean.

teach.topic: Main parts of an offshore platform
teach.model: The jacket is a steel frame on the sea bed that holds up the topsides, where the equipment sits. A derrick drills, cranes lift, a flare burns spare gas, and a blowout preventer seals the well in an emergency. Anodes protect steel from corrosion.

points.ask: What stops an emergency from the well?

stages.title: Subsea production systems
stages.hook: Some oil and gas wells are 1500 m below the surface, where people cannot work. How do they get the oil to the top?
explain: A subsea production system puts the equipment on the sea floor instead of on a platform. Each well has a wellhead and a Christmas tree, a block of valves that controls the flow. Pipes called flowlines carry the oil and gas from the trees to a manifold, which gathers the flows of several wells.

From the manifold, a flowline and a riser (a pipe rising to the surface) bring the fluids to a host platform or a floating vessel. An umbilical, a bundle of tubes and cables, carries electricity, hydraulic fluid and chemicals down from the surface to operate valves.

Everything must be built for high pressure and cold water. At 1500 m, p = ρgh ≈ 15 MPa. Cold water can cause hydrates (ice-like solids of gas and water) that block pipes, so chemicals such as methanol are injected and pipes are insulated. ROVs, robot submarines, do the underwater work.

example.q: Find the water pressure at 1500 m (ρ = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²) in MPa.

analogies.home: The Christmas tree is like the tap and valves on a water supply, controlling the flow.
analogies.city: A manifold is like a junction where several roads join into one.
analogies.tech: An ROV is a drone for the deep, steered from the ship with a cable.
analogies.farm: An umbilical is like the cables and hoses of a milking machine, bringing power and fluids to the equipment.

stages.mnemonic: Well, tree, manifold, flowline, riser: up it goes. The umbilical sends orders down.
terms: A set of valves on top of a well controlling the flow.
A unit that gathers flows from several wells.
A bundle of tubes and cables for control and chemicals.
An ice-like solid made of gas and water that can block pipes.

misc.wrong: Subsea equipment can be fixed easily if it breaks.
misc.right: Repairs need ROVs or special ships, which are expensive and weather-dependent, so equipment is designed to be very reliable.

stages.limits: Details differ between fields. Some use many wells connected to far-away hosts, called tiebacks. Decisions depend on cost, depth and distance.

trip.prompt: Look at a layout diagram. Follow the path from a well to the surface.

questions.q: What is a manifold?
o: A unit that gathers flow from several wells
A kind of ship that carries cargo to the rigs
A tide table that lists high and low water
A crane that lifts parts from a supply boat
questions.why: It joins flowlines from several wells into one.

questions.q: What does a riser do?
o: Carries fluids up to the surface
Holds the anchor
Measures tides
Floats the ship
questions.why: A riser connects the seabed system to the surface.

questions.q: What is carried in an umbilical?
o: Power, hydraulic fluid and chemicals
Oil only
Fish
Sand
questions.why: It controls the subsea valves and delivers chemicals.

questions.q: Why are hydrates a problem in subsea pipes?
o: Ice-like solids can block the flow
They make the oil hot enough to burn the pipe
They sink the ship that lays the pipes
They stop rust and so the pipe becomes too strong
questions.why: Cold, high-pressure conditions let gas and water form solid blockages.

questions.q: A subsea pipe is stopped for several days in cold water. Which action best prevents hydrates?
o: Inject methanol and keep the pipe insulated
Add more water to the pipe to wash it out
Switch off all chemicals to save money
Cool it faster so the pipe settles
questions.why: Methanol changes hydrate conditions and insulation keeps the fluid warm.

questions.q: Use ρ = 1025 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s². What is the water pressure at 1500 m depth, in MPa (1 decimal place)?
Oil flows through a 12 km flowline at 2 m/s. How many minutes does it take to travel the whole line?
Order the path of oil from the reservoir to the surface.
questions.why: Fluid leaves the well through the tree to the manifold, then up the riser.

questions.q: Match each part to its role.
questions.why: Each part has its own job.

questions.q: Why do engineers use robots (ROVs) rather than divers for subsea work in very deep water?
questions.model: At great depth the pressure and cold are too dangerous for divers. A robot controlled from a ship can work there safely.
questions.why: Great depth is beyond safe human diving, so ROVs are used.

panel.q: A control valve on the Christmas tree is designed to close if the umbilical loses hydraulic pressure. What is this called?
o: Fail-safe design
Luck
Anode
Hydrate
panel.why: Fail-safe means the valve goes to the safe (closed) position on failure.

panel.q: A subsea leak is found. Why is it vital to stop and report it quickly?
o: Oil can harm sea life over a wide area
Oil is tasty to fish and brings them in
It heats the ocean for miles around the leak
Leaks fix themselves, but only after some days
panel.why: Early action limits environmental damage.

panel.q: Why do operators prefer subsea systems for deep water fields?
o: A fixed platform would be too expensive at that depth
Subsea is always cheaper at every depth
Platforms are illegal in deep water
Fish prefer it, so catches would get larger
panel.why: At great depth, fixed platforms become impractical, so subsea tiebacks are used.

teach.topic: How oil gets from a deep well to the surface
teach.model: Oil flows from the well through a Christmas tree of valves, then along flowlines to a manifold that collects flows. A riser carries it up to a platform or ship. An umbilical sends power and chemicals down, and robots do repairs.
